meta.title: Midterm Blood Bath, $4T AI Sell Off, Data Center Freeze, What’s Next for Trump
meta.speakers: Jason Calacanis, David Sacks, Chamath Palihapitiya, David Friedberg
meta.thread_line: 6 threads · why the midterms were a rout · Trump's path back · the data-center permit freeze · the SpaceX–Anthropic compute lever · AI regulation and power · OpenAI's exponential-time result

snapshot: Democrats took both chambers (Senate **54-56**, House at least 250) and 29+ governorships; Texas, Kansas, Iowa and South Carolina flipped.
Sacks blames the Iran war: gas from $3 to over $4, inflation back from **2.4% to 3.7%**, mortgages near 7.5%, and the podcaster base lost.
Chamath admits a blind spot: the economy is broken for wage earners, and voters now swing violently against whoever holds power.
A **$4 trillion** AI selloff hit Nvidia, SpaceX, Tesla, AMD and Micron; Polymarket odds of an OpenAI IPO this year fell from 95% to 71%.
Sacks expects fully permitted data centers to finish in 2027 but a thin new-project pipeline by **2028**, since no politician gains from signing permits.
Chamath calls hyperscalers the kingmakers and says the 90-day termination clause in SpaceX's Anthropic compute deal could reprice it 2-3x.
Friedberg warns governments will regulate compute and treat data centers as utilities; Sacks expects a federal AI department; Jason puts it at 1%.
Science corner: an OpenAI paper of 175 pages claims 3-SAT is solvable in subexponential time, refuting the 1999 exponential time hypothesis; still under review.

themes.title: The midterm rout: war-driven inflation, or a broken economy?
themes.lead: All four agree affordability decided the vote; they split on whether the Iran war caused it or only exposed it.
bullets: Results: Democrats at **54, 55 or 56** Senate seats (Alaska, Mississippi still counting), at least 250-260 House seats, 29+ governorships; Republicans lost ground with every group, even white men.

Sacks: gas rose from about $3 to over $4, diesel higher; inflation went from 2.4% in January to 3.7%, rate cuts turned into a hike, mortgages hit about 7.5%; families pay **$200** a month more on fuel.

Sacks' charts: Trump's net approval tracks the gas price; the Senate prediction market only turned after the war began on **February 28, 2026**; 34% called the war decisive and 40% significant, so 74% in all.

Sacks admits he expected a 'red splash': jobs strong, unemployment 4.1%, GDP 2.1-2.5% in H1 and 3.7% in Q3 per GDPNow, real household income up 3.1% in year one; young men swung **36 points** and the podcasters (Tucker Carlson, Joe Rogan, Theo Von, Tim Dillon, Megyn Kelly) left.

Jason: the slide began before the war; per Nate Silver's **Silver Bulletin**, approval went from +5 to -28, via Liberation Day tariffs (lost at the Supreme Court), masked ICE raids, and the Epstein files; he now votes 55/45 Democrat, from 70/30.
Chamath: money and gerrymandering failed (of **15** redrawn Republican districts, Democrats won 11); centrists focused only on affordability won, so ideology matters less than a broken economy.

Friedberg: the end of DOGE on **June 5, 2025** ('China just won') left a $7 trillion budget with a $2 trillion deficit; costs keep rising, so voters drift to socialist policies without choosing socialism.

quote.text: It was a rout. It was a devastating blow. It , I believe, the biggest defeat on midterm elections since Watergate.

themes.watch: Sacks served in the Trump administration and argues its record from the inside; Jason replayed his own pre-war prediction clip, which Sacks called a stopped clock.

themes.title: Trump's path back: end the war, then strike populist deals
themes.lead: Everyone puts ending the Iran war first; beyond that the prescriptions run from tax deals to blanket pardons.
bullets: Sacks: Brent fell **10%** on Election Day as markets priced an end to the war; he sees it going from about $117-110 to $70, and Trump's approval back above 40%.

Sacks' precedents: Clinton (1994) and Obama (2010, minus 7 Senate and 63 House seats) adjusted and won again; Bush doubled down with the Iraq surge after 2006 and Republicans lost 2008; neocons now push a similar escalation.

Jason's five-point plan: pardon everyone now; tax margin loans over **$10 million** at 50% capital gains, credited back on repayment; a health plan; $15 minimum wage via $2 a year for four years (only 10-15 million earn under $15); a stock-trading ban for officials (Rahm Emanuel's idea); a housing-construction plan.
Chamath: zero federal tax on income under about $150k (later $125k), end federal loan guarantees with student-debt cancellation, close loopholes; trade those for keeping the border closed.
Chamath: like Reagan, tariffs plus allocated funds could look better as domestic production builds; the 2028 winner will run on **economic populism**, left or right.
Friedberg expects Congress and the President to fail to agree a budget in 2027, so costs keep rising; the bond market will signal where it goes.

quote.text: Just get out of the war. Okay, stop the war. This is my number one, number two and number three.

themes.watch: Brent and approval targets are Sacks' conditional view, tied to the war ending quickly.

themes.title: The data-center freeze: 2027 capex holds, the 2028 pipeline thins
themes.lead: Data centers became the voters' symbol of oligarchy, and Sacks thinks no politician will sign new permits for years.
bullets: About **$4 trillion** of market cap was erased early in the week, the worst day in dollar terms; it overshadowed the Anthropic IPO.

Polymarket odds of an OpenAI IPO this year fell to **71%** from 95% before the midterms; the WSJ reports a valuation near $1 trillion versus $1.5-2 trillion (and Gavin Baker's $3-4 trillion on this podcast).
Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa beat Abbott on economic populism, tying data centers to higher utility bills and water use; she says no new permits until legislation passes.
Sacks disagrees with Gavin Baker's calm read; a **SemiAnalysis** analyst notes projects under construction may still lack final permits (e.g. air emissions), risking half-finished sites.
Sacks' base case: fully permitted projects finish in 2027, but by **2028** the pipeline is closed or sharply reduced; both parties ran ads attacking politicians who approved data centers.
Sacks: a gigawatt data center costs about **$50 billion**, and nobody commits that under injunction or protest risk; he expects Democrats to blame Trump for a 2028 capex drop.
Chamath: a SpaceX team (Riley and Katie) pitched a 6 GW site in Cochise County, Arizona (40% lower power costs, no water, 20% lower property taxes) and was shouted down; it is emotional, not factual.

Jason: blocked projects move to Canada, Mexico, Singapore, Malaysia (where Google is building a huge one) or the Gulf after the war, making the US a **net importer of tokens** and losing $300-400k construction jobs.

quote.text: No one can make such investments in under conditions of uncertainty.

themes.title: Scarce compute makes hyperscalers kingmakers, and one 90-day clause the key move
themes.lead: Chamath argues a slowdown helps those who already own capacity and squeezes tenants: neoclouds and frontier labs.
bullets: Winners: **Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, Google, SpaceX** own the capacity; neoclouds and foundation-model labs are tenants and at risk.
Option two: hyperscalers keep new capacity for their own models (Google to Gemini) to slow Anthropic and OpenAI, which improve on 60-90 day cycles.
The 'crazy way': the **SpaceX–Anthropic** compute deal has a mutual 90-day termination; repricing at spot could lift SpaceX's Anthropic revenue 2-3x and force capitulation.
That move would push neoclouds to buy all compute they can at any price, or face bankruptcy.
Signal: Chamath says **Google** just took control of a Crusoe data center and evicted the tenant, because it holds power and other key resources.
Jason disagrees: Elon's close ties to Anthropic and hostility toward Sam Altman make a middle compromise likelier; Chamath says it is math, and rising spot prices make old contracts unprofitable.

Chamath: if building slows, cost per megawatt-month and GPU-hour soar; capacity could go to Google or Meta. Friedberg adds compute both serves users and trains the next model, so Google, Microsoft or Nvidia hoarding it could decide the frontier.
themes.watch: The SpaceX repricing is Chamath's game-theory scenario, not a reported plan; Jason argues the relationship makes it unlikely.

themes.title: Who controls AI: compute rules, a federal AI department, or regulatory capture
themes.lead: Friedberg and Sacks fear state control of AI; Chamath expects a deal that favors incumbents; Jason calls it Doctor Doom.
bullets: Friedberg: AI is like **Sauron's ring**; governments will regulate compute rather than chips or models, and treat data centers as public utilities.
Friedberg: models are code and a free-speech question; existing laws already cover misuse; a state with better AI than its citizens is a Second Amendment-style power gap.

Jason puts Friedberg's scenario at about **1%**; left politicians want to ban data centers, models and their use; California passed a bill Newsom vetoed, and states pass a patchwork of hundreds of laws.
Sacks: it is **100%** clear Democrats push AI legislation; a federal Department of AI pre-approving frontier models would build a surveillance and censorship state, like COVID-era social media.
Sacks: federal level handles AI safety; infrastructure gets decided at state and local level.

Chamath: no nationalization; expect 'service for service', with more power for government and regulatory moats for closed-model duopolies, while Meta, Amazon, Google, Microsoft and SpaceX stay the real owners.
Friedberg: Gallup finds **93%** of Chinese optimistic on AI versus 36% of Americans, fourth from the bottom, below Afghanistan; that made the oligarch narrative easy.

quote.text: I believe that the Democrats want to create a surveillance and censorship state, reinforced superintelligence.

themes.watch: Sacks was the administration's AI lead, so his view of Democratic AI policy is that of an opponent.

themes.title: OpenAI says it refuted the exponential time hypothesis
themes.lead: Friedberg presents an OpenAI paper claiming 3-SAT can be solved in subexponential time, a 27-year-old open question.
bullets: The 1999 exponential time hypothesis says 3-SAT needs time exponential in problem size.
OpenAI's **175-page** paper claims a subexponential method; done in under 10 days, some reports say hours.
Friedberg reads it as keeping P = NP possible, meaning any problem could in theory be computed.
The proof is still being assessed by outside researchers.
Sacks: AI will bring many benefits; if the US doesn't build it, China will, and the US will import tokens.

quote.text: this is one of those moments of humility for mathematicians

takeaways.title: Use Brent as the gauge of an Iran exit: Sacks sees $70 if the war ends
Favor owners of permitted capacity over compute tenants while permits freeze
Plan for a 2028 capex air pocket, not a 2027 one
Track the SpaceX–Anthropic 90-day clause and any federal AI department bill
Read 2028 through economic populism, not left versus right

other_news.title: All-In's election-night stream drew about **500,000** live viewers, versus 87,000 for far-right and 250,000 for far-left streamers; guests included Ted Cruz, Rahm Emanuel, Polymarket's Shayne Coplan, Tim Dillon, Taylor Lorenz, Brad Gerstner and Ben Shapiro.

Reactions: Ted Cruz called it Watergate-level rejection, DeSantis 'about to the level of extinction'; JD Vance's post named the Iran war and urged ending it, cost of living, America First and a shift on Israel.

Jason's firm **Launch** (20 staff, ~100 investments a year) spends $40-50k a year on Grok and Claude, estimates $2M of value (15-21x return), and plans a Mac Studio 512K ($20k each, ~$400k) for local models; he says only 10-20% of corporate America uses AI daily.
Chamath recorded a barefoot interview at Rick Rubin's studio; Rubin asked what the show's 'magic' is, and Chamath says it is honesty.

Sources referenced: Polymarket, Nate Silver's Silver Bulletin, Gallup, GDPNow, the Wall Street Journal, SemiAnalysis, Gavin Baker, the New York Times interview with Hinojosa, the CEO of Cuts Clothing, and the SpaceX Cochise County video on X.
